narrative:
The model estimates a 70% chance that you will leave, so it treats you as a high turnover risk and, because promotion decisions are tied to that prediction, you are denied a promotion. This is a forecast, not a verdict on your performance.

The strongest factor worked in your favor: your total experience of one to five years pushed the estimate toward staying, as this range is common among employees predicted to stay. The next most important factor worked against you: you reported other job opportunities, and only about a quarter of employees predicted to stay had such opportunities. That outside option makes leaving more plausible. The third factor, psychological exhaustion, added a smaller push toward leaving; although you reported none, which is common in the stay group, it did not offset the turnover signal in your overall profile.

Your profile also includes lower satisfaction with pay relative to effort, no annual bonus, no felt job stability, and no sense of deserved promotion. These reinforce the risk. Before finalizing denial, consider whether a high leave risk should prompt retention action rather than automatic exclusion. Discuss clearer promotion criteria, reward and stability improvements, and whether external opportunities can be addressed. Ask for specific feedback on what would make promotion viable and what support would reduce turnover risk. The organization should review whether denying promotion because of predicted departure is appropriate and whether it could worsen the very risk it predicts.
